issues.legal_issue: The limitation rule for cancelling an instrument depends on whether the instrument is voidable or void ab initio.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought relief concerning a sale deed and alleged fraudulent misrepresentation about its contents, not its character.
The plaintiff was found to have been a minor when the deed was executed, and the deed was treated as void on that basis.
issues.conclusion: Article 59 applies to claims to cancel prima facie valid, voidable instruments where fraud or mistake must be proved; it does not apply to an instrument that is void ab initio. A suit seeking cancellation is nevertheless subject to limitation, including the residuary limitation rule where Article 59 does not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to voidable transactions and instruments that are prima facie valid, including claims requiring proof of fraud or mistake; it does not govern presumptively invalid instruments that are void ab initio. Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides for discretionary cancellation of void or voidable instruments. The Court relied on Unni v. Kunchi Amma and Sheo Shankar Gir v. Ram Shewak Chowdhri for the distinction between void and voidable instruments, and on Ningawwa v. Byrappa Shiddappa Hireknrabnar for the distinction between fraudulent misrepresentation about a document’s character and about its contents. It also noted that Article 59 combined the scope of former Articles 91 and 114.

predicates.instrument_cancellation_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking cancellation of a written instrument.
predicates.instrument_is_voidable: The instrument is prima facie valid but may be avoided on a ground requiring proof.
predicates.fraud_or_mistake_requires_proof: The claimant relies on fraud or mistake that must be proved to obtain relief.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks cancellation of a prima facie valid instrument on a ground requiring proof of fraud or mistake, the claim is subject to the limitation rule for setting aside instruments.

issues.legal_issue: A claim based on a void deed is not exempt from limitation, and a minor who seeks to recover property conveyed by such a deed must sue within one of the applicable periods.
material_facts: The plaintiff was about twelve years old when the sale deed was executed in 1961 and attained majority in 1969.
The plaintiff filed suit in 1979, after both twelve years from execution of the deed and three years from attaining majority had elapsed.
The trial court dismissed the suit as barred by limitation, while the appellate court and High Court held it was not barred.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation because it was filed neither within twelve years of the deed nor within three years of the plaintiff attaining majority; the trial court’s dismissal was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires dismissal of a suit instituted after the prescribed period, whether or not limitation is pleaded. Limitation ordinarily bars the remedy rather than extinguishing the right, subject to the exception in Section 27 concerning suits for possession. A void transaction does not make the Limitation Act wholly inapplicable. The Court held that a minor whose property was purportedly conveyed by a void deed could sue within twelve years of the deed or within three years of attaining majority. It relied on P.C.K. Muthia Chettiar v. V.E.S. Shanmugham Chettiar concerning limitation in cases of fraud, and distinguished the principle in Balvant N. Viswamitra v. Yadav Sadashiv Mule, which concerned a void decree challenged in execution or collateral proceedings.

rule.if: minor_deed_property_recovery_suit and deed_executed_during_minority and not filed_within_twelve_years_of_deed and not filed_within_three_years_after_majority

predicates.minor_deed_property_recovery_suit: A claimant brought a suit to recover property purportedly conveyed by a deed executed while the claimant was a minor.
predicates.deed_executed_during_minority: The deed was executed while the claimant was under the age of majority.
predicates.filed_within_twelve_years_of_deed: The claimant filed suit within twelve years after execution of the deed.
predicates.filed_within_three_years_after_majority: The claimant filed suit within three years after attaining majority.

issues.definition: A property-recovery suit based on a deed executed during the claimant’s minority is barred when it was filed neither within twelve years of the deed nor within three years after majority.

issues.legal_issue: A registered instrument is presumed to have been validly executed unless the party challenging it rebuts that presumption.
material_facts: The plaintiff challenged the sale deed.
The deed was treated as a registered document, and the plaintiff failed to rebut the presumption of valid execution.
issues.conclusion: The presumption that the registered deed was validly executed stood unrebutted, and the burden of rebutting it rested on the plaintiff.
issues.legal_principle: A registered document is presumed to have been validly executed and is prima facie valid in law; the party adducing evidence to challenge it bears the burden of rebutting that presumption.

predicates.registered_instrument_challenged: A party brought a claim challenging an instrument that had been registered.
predicates.challenger_fails_to_rebut_valid_executio: The party challenging the instrument did not rebut the presumption that it was validly executed.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a registered instrument but does not rebut the presumption of valid execution, the instrument is presumed to have been validly executed.
